new_statements.quote: 2.11 Word or syllable stress is not significant in any of the languages studied here. The spoken context runs smooth without emphasis of any syllable unless in cases of long vowels (or diphthongs), besides not very frequent in the Gunggari languages. As usual, in a spoken context or sequence of syllables, however, the second initial syllable often carries mechanically more stress than the others (cf. in Part I, 2.9), which explains the origin of such shortened forms as ge· (Gun EA) for jingia where?; this tendency is frequently reflected in the current pronunciation of place names of several syllables, derived from Aboriginal words, in Queensland: Barálba, Mundúbbera etc.
new_statements.citation: Holmer, Nils M. 1983. Linguistic survey of south-eastern Queensland. Pacific Linguistics D-54. Canberra: Australian National University.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not phonologically significant in any language of Holmer's 'Gunggari group' (Gunggari/Roma language, Bidjara, Marganj, Gangulu, Wirri, Birri, Ngawun); in connected speech or longer words the second syllable tends to carry mechanically more prominence than the others.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated for this group; Part I 2.9 (p. 5) and the Bidjara remark (p. ~184) speak of secondary stress on subsequent alternate syllables after the second-syllable prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: Long vowels or diphthongs attract emphasis ('unless in cases of long vowels (or diphthongs)'); shortened forms like ge· for jingia 'where?' explained by the second-syllable tendency.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level statement covering connected speech and words ('spoken context or sequence of syllables'); not specific to Mandandanyi: Holmer's Gunggari informants were Roma-born (Tottie Carbine, Liza Malone, Bill Tobane's father, Queenie Long) and he places the language at Roma, Mitchell, Taroom, Surat, Charleville, which is Mandandanji country, but the name Mandandanji never occurs. Identical statement already credited to kung1258 (Gunggari D37) in this reading.
new_statements.identity_note: The only statement found is Holmer 1983's group-level claim for 'the Gunggari languages', whose principal member 'Gunggari, or the Roma language' was recorded from Roma-born speakers and located at Roma, Mitchell, Taroom, Surat and Charleville - the Maranoa/Roma country that Curr no. 174, Ridley's 'Kogai' and Mathews' 'Kogai' assign to Mandandanji, and AIATSIS's alternate names for D44 include 'Maranoa Gunggari' and 'Eastern Gunggari'. Holmer never uses the name Mandandanji, and this reading has already credited the same sentence to kung1258 (Kunggari/Gunggari, AIATSIS D37). Treat as a shared Southern Maric (sout2765) group statement, not an independent Mandandanyi description; do not count it twice.

sources.note: 2.11 p.178: 'Word or syllable stress is not significant in any of the languages studied here' (Gunggari group = Gunggari, Bidjara, Marganj, Gangulu, Wirri, Birri, Ngawun); a mechanical tendency to more stress on the second syllable in longer sequences.
